articles.title: Budget 2026: experts on what John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ plan means for households
articles.author: Alper Kara, Head of Department of Economics, Finance & Accounting, Brunel University of London
paras: It was a “breathing space” budget from Chancellor John Healey. In the absence of big surprises or bold change, Healey’s trade-off appears to be small reliefs now in exchange for “fresh hope” in the future. Here’s what our experts made of the chancellor’s first budget.
Targeted help with energy costs as bills keep rising
Jonquil Lowe, Visiting Academic, The Open University

This budget took place against a backdrop of global turmoil and rising inflation, driven largely by higher energy costs. These are continuing to squeeze household budgets. From January, the energy price cap is predicted to rise by 27% to nearly £2,200 a year for a typical household.

Help with energy costs is therefore an important move. This support includes a £100 energy payment for households in England in council tax bands A to D (the devolved governments will receive equivalent funding to replicate this).

There was also a commitment to abolish the standing charge for gas (currently on average 30 pence a day). The amount will instead be added to the charge for the unit cost of each kilowatt-hour used. This gives households more control over their bills – it will mean that limiting the amount of gas they use will have a bigger effect on reducing their cost. However, one worry is that squeezed households could still risk their health by not heating their homes adequately.

Labour’s manifesto pledged not to raise taxes on working people. This budget technically kept to that if we assume that working people just receive earnings. But building on last year’s changes, this budget has introduced another increase to the tax rates on interest from savings and rental income. Landlords and some savers will be taxed at a basic rate of 24% (currently 20%), higher rate 44% (from 40%) and additional rate 49% (from 45%) from April 2027.

This makes it all the more welcome that a proposal last year to cut the cash ISA limit for savers aged under 65 to £12,000 is being abandoned. Everyone, regardless of their age, will still be able to put up to £20,000 a year into a cash ISA (or cash and money funds within a stocks-and-shares ISA) and receive the interest tax-free.

The government will also consult on setting up a first-time buyer ISA to replace the Lifetime ISA and help people save for a home. From February 2027, a new scheme called Your First Home will provide equity loans for first-time buyers purchasing new properties. The loan, worth 20% of the purchase price, will be tax-free for the first five years. To be eligible buyers must have a household income of no more than £110,000 (£140,000 in London).

The budget also delivered a higher tax-free personal allowance for pensioners on the lowest incomes. The new Pension Tax Allowance will be applied automatically, with HMRC doing the sums. Pensioners with income up to £13,037 (the full state pension) will pay no income tax from April 2027. For comparison, for younger people the standard allowance is frozen at £12,570 until April 2031. They would pay £93.40 tax on an income of £13,037.

The announcements come on top of a drip feed of “everyday fixes” in the days leading up to the budget. These included reform of carer’s allowance so that carers no longer lose their whole allowance of £86.45 a week once their earnings pass a weekly limit of £204. But it has already emerged that this much-touted change will not come into effect until 2030 while the government updates its IT systems.
Small clues that this government is chasing growth
Maha Rafi Atal, Adam Smith Senior Lecturer in Political Economy, University of Glasgow

For years, the UK has faced a structural deadlock: a public that demands robust state services, but which rejects both the broad-based income taxes and pro-growth measures like increased immigration that might fund those services. Under Rachel Reeves’ chancellorship, Labour tried to get around this by raising the necessary taxes indirectly – from everywhere but income. This made it more expensive for businesses to operate, failing to jumpstart growth.

In this budget, John Healey has tried a different tack, deploying selective business reliefs alongside a commitment to increased defence spending. Together, these measures make a calculated gamble that state stimulus can rescue the economy from lacklustre growth. In a growing economy, the government gets more tax revenue to fund services even without raising rates, because there’s more economic activity to tax in the first place.

The reliefs for business are welcome. Raising the small business rate relief threshold – effectively removing half of all shops, restaurants and gyms from the rates system – provides breathing room for local economies. When paired with the electricity bill reduction for core industries and the introduction of “founders’ relief” for entrepreneurs selling shares in their business, the budget offers some incentives for corporate investment and entrepreneurial risk.

The chancellor has also listened in part to businesses that complained of rising costs as a result of the increase in employers’ national insurance and the new measures in the Employment Rights Act. While the minimum wage is set to rise, the government has restored a lower rate for younger workers. This will benefit some businesses in employing people more cheaply, but the government also hopes it will help absorb school-leavers and graduates into the workforce, increasing productivity and reducing the welfare bill.

The budget introduces two distinct avenues for the state to proactively stimulate growth. First, through accelerated defence commitments (spending 3% of GDP by 2030, for example), the chancellor is injecting capital directly into domestic supply chains, manufacturing, and high-tech engineering. Second, the roadmap for fiscal devolution offers a regional stimulus by promising to let mayors keep 100% of local business rates by the end of the decade, as well as a share of income tax receipts. This kind of arrangement, to fund infrastructure and attract business, is standard practice in most federalised systems. But its absence has been an unusual quirk of UK devolution.

Yet, while these measures are constructive, it is not clear that they are enough to reverse the grim reality: growth is stagnant at just over 1% and the Office for Budget Responsibility predicts it will stay that way.

Unlike its predecessor, this government seems to accept that it desperately needs some growth, and therefore some private investment, or public services will fall apart. In this budget, it has signaled some understanding that it may have to meet business halfway to get there. But the fiscal forecast relies on the hope that these stimuli will take effect in time to expand the tax base and preserve public spending before the next election.

If they do not, the Treasury has also signaled that like Reeves before him, Healey will resort to spending cuts in the final years of the parliament to balance the books. By deferring that choice, the government has chosen to pray for a growth miracle today, while keeping the threat of real-terms austerity on the horizon tomorrow.
Banks to pay more – but Healey bids to keep them lending
Alper Kara, Professor of Banking and Finance, Brunel University of London

One surprise is the relatively modest increase in taxes on banks compared with what financial markets had been expecting. There had been speculation that the government would raise the surcharge on bank profits from 3% to 8%. Instead, the surcharge will increase to 6% for just 15 months, from January 2027. So banks will face a higher tax bill, but a smaller one than many investors had feared.

Shares in some major UK banks rose as investors welcomed the smaller-than-expected increase. This suggests that investors believe the profitability of banks will be less affected by the tax increase than previously feared.

But the decision also reflects the difficult balance facing the chancellor. The government needs more money to support public spending and manage its finances, particularly at a time when borrowing costs remain high. Banks are an attractive source of revenue because their profits have been relatively strong in recent years.

And since 2023, higher interest rates have helped many banks earn more. These profits come from the difference between what banks charge borrowers and what they pay savers. So, the government has a reasonable argument that banks should make a greater contribution to public finances. This is especially true when households and businesses have been struggling with high living costs.

However, the amount of additional revenue matters. Taxing banks more will generate £1.5 billion in extra income for the Treasury, but it is unlikely to make a substantial difference to the government’s wider spending commitments, such as defence. A temporary increase also means that the additional revenue cannot be relied upon over the longer term.

And the next question is who will ultimately pay for this tax increase. Banks could absorb the additional cost through lower profits and reduced returns to shareholders. Alternatively, they might try to protect their profitability by offering lower savings rates, charging higher interest rates on new mortgages and business loans, or increasing fees for customers.

However, competition in the banking market will limit how much of the tax banks can pass on to customers. Banks that increase mortgage rates or reduce savings rates risk losing customers to competitors. Given that the surcharge increase will last only 15 months, my view is that banks may prefer to absorb much of the additional cost rather than risk losing market share.

The chancellor’s decision to keep the annual cash ISA allowance at £20,000, rather than reducing it to £12,000 as previously planned could also help banks. Cash ISA deposits are an important source of funding for banks and building societies, particularly for mortgage lending.

Keeping the higher allowance could help banks retain those deposits and avoid additional funding pressures. This may also be part of the chancellor’s attempt to balance higher bank taxes with the need to keep banks lending to households and businesses.

There are also wider considerations. Higher taxes could affect the international competitiveness of the UK banking sector, as banks consider taxation when deciding where to expand their operations. Sustained higher taxation could discourage investment in the UK banking sector, potentially leading to fewer new jobs or even job losses over the longer term.

By opting for a smaller and temporary increase, the chancellor appears to have recognised these risks. His decision seems to be aimed at a balance between raising additional revenue and limiting the impact on lending and investment.
Relief on energy bills could remove push for heat pumps
Dylan Ryan, Lecturer in Mechanical & Energy Engineering, Edinburgh Napier University
The overall cost of heating with gas will drop for most people, except for those with larger homes, after the chancellor’s announcement.

Once the standing charge, a fixed daily fee, is removed, gas bills will reflect what people actually use. While these lower-than-expected bills will be a welcome relief for bill payers, it could weaken the economic case for households to switch to using heat pumps.

There had been rumours of cuts to the boiler upgrade scheme intended to help more home owners install heat pumps. However, that didn’t happen. A government report on the scheme said that 65% of property owners who installed heat pumps did so because this grant was available. The report also pointed out that 52% of all recipients of the grant were large detached four-bedroom or bigger homes. So, some sort of reform could be needed.
The cut to VAT on electricity and the £100 paid to those in bands A-D homes will also provide some relief for energy bill-payers.

However, energy prices are expected to rise again by the next price cap adjustment in January 2027, due to the Iran war pushing up global energy prices. The government may need to provide some additional relief then. For example, further decoupling electricity prices from the price of gas, as gas often sets the price for electricity.
Ultimately, moving energy use away from fossil fuels is a balancing act. But the government is going to have to make further changes if it expects to meet its climate change targets by 2050.

articles.title: We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth
articles.author: Simon Buechler, Assistant Professor of Finance, Miami University
paras: Data centers require enormous investments: land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure. Yet, once they’re up and running, they tend to employ no more than a few dozen people in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are asking what they will get in return.

Skepticism about the local benefits of data centers is contributing to growing opposition to their construction, from Ohio to Texas. That pushback contributed to delays or cancellations of US$156 billion in proposed data center projects in 2025 alone.

We are professors who study real estate and urban economics, including how large place-based investments shape local economies. So we set out to answer a question at the center of these fights: Do data centers actually create jobs where they are built?

To find out, we teamed up with four colleagues to study what happens to local employment after data centers open. We found that new data centers that opened from 2000-2023 created 1,000 to 1,300 jobs in the counties where they are located, on average. But those jobs, which are for work performed outside data centers rather than inside them, take a few years to appear. They are mostly in industries that support data centers, not in restaurants or shops.
How data centers create local jobs
Data centers can create jobs in at least three ways beyond employing people who work inside them.
First, they can increase demand for local suppliers, from security companies that protect the facilities to electrical contractors that maintain their equipment.
Second, data center employees and workers at these suppliers may spend more money locally, supporting restaurants, stores and other local services.

Third, companies already operating data centers may expand their facilities, while other operators may decide to build nearby. Once a location has the electricity, fiber connections and other infrastructure needed to operate a data center, further investment may become easier.
Tracking data centers and jobs

We assembled detailed information on 1,584 U.S. data centers that opened between 2000 and 2023. For each facility, we recorded its location, opening date and power capacity, which is a standard way to compare facilities of different sizes. We then matched these records with federal data on employment, wages and the number of businesses in each county.

Isolating the effect of data centers isn’t straightforward. Operators don’t choose locations randomly. They look for reliable electricity, fiber connections, available land and friendly local regulations. Those places may already be growing, so new jobs might have appeared even without a data center.

To account for this, we tracked employment in counties that received data centers – such as Loudoun County in Virginia, Berkeley County in South Carolina, Morrow County in Oregon, and others – before and after the operation of the facility began. We then compared those trends with similar counties that did not receive data centers. We also looked at whether larger facilities brought bigger job gains.
Jobs appear, but not immediately

During the first two years after a county’s first data center opened, we found little change in employment outside construction. After that, jobs begin to grow. Three to five years after a center opened, we found that these counties had roughly 1,000 to 1,300 additional nonconstruction jobs than comparable counties without data centers.
Bigger investments brought bigger employment gains. Five years after new data center capacity is installed, each additional megawatt is associated with about 7.4 more nonconstruction local jobs.

Part of that gain, however, reflects further expansion. Each megawatt installed is associated with another 1.7 megawatts of capacity over the following years. Once that later growth is counted, our estimates work out to about 2.7 nonconstruction jobs per megawatt of eventual data center capacity. A large 100-megawatt facility, for example, would be correlated with roughly 275 additional local jobs outside the data center itself.
Jobs are not where you might expect
The types of jobs created help explain what is happening.

Employment gains are concentrated in transportation and warehousing, professional and technical services and real estate. These industries may serve or benefit directly from data centers or from the investment and infrastructure they bring.
By contrast, we found little evidence of job growth in restaurants, stores and other local services.

We also found that more data center investment tends to follow in the same county. Most often, the companies already operating in a county expand their facilities. Other companies generally don’t move into that same area to build new data centers.
Jobs are only one side of the equation

Our study has limits. It covers data centers that opened through 2023, before the current wave of massive facilities were built to power AI. Larger data centers do not necessarily create proportionally more jobs, so our findings may not apply to today’s biggest projects.

We also looked only at job gains and did not explore whether data centers are worth their cost to local communities. These facilities consume large amounts of electricity and water, can generate noise and may receive substantial tax breaks from local and state governments. We did not address any of those concerns.

Our findings do show that data centers can create jobs beyond the small number of people working inside their walls. But that does not mean every one of them is a good deal for their local community. And whether those additional jobs justify the costs remains an open question.

articles.title: Victorian spiritualism capitalised on the desire to transcend death to create new ways of making money
articles.author: James Cronin, Professor in Marketing and Consumer Culture Studies, Lancaster University
paras: Death has never entirely stopped the living from trying to continue a conversation with their loved ones.

Today, AI-powered deathbots and a growing range of “grief tech” bring to market several ways that consumers can recreate the voices of the deceased. They open new commercial opportunities and experiences alongside uncomfortable questions about whether grief should be profitable.

Yet long before AI made it possible to simulate (and charge a premium for) a familiar voice, the spiritualist movement that swept across Victorian Britain negotiated issues of credibility, authenticity and commercial exploitation while transforming one of humanity’s most enduring desires into something marketable.
Our research into the business history of spiritualism in 19th-century Britain suggests that the similarities go deeper than a shared fascination with communicating with the dead.

Victorian Britain is often remembered as an age of industrial progress, scientific discovery and astonishing feats of engineering. Department stores, arcades and luxury brands fed a growing appetite for shopping. Yet the Victorians were also fascinated by ghosts, the supernatural and the macabre.

These tendencies might first be written off as a contradiction – the perseverance of premodern supernaturalism among an increasingly modern society. But a closer look reveals that the technologies that transformed Victorian commerce and entertainment also helped make ghosts visible, reproducible and profitable.

Large-scale plate glass production, advances in illumination, and optical physics (the scientific study of how light behaves and interacts with matter around us) allowed for the staging of phantasmagorical illusions like Pepper’s Ghost, while photography could apparently capture the dead. Gothic fiction prospered and cheap paperbacks called penny dreadfuls traded heavily in tales of the strange, the sordid and the supernatural.

The supernatural was not simply surviving on the margins of industrial modernity; it was finding new opportunities within it. The philosopher Slavoj Žižek offers a useful explanation, arguing that societies are sustained partly through an “underside” of practices and desires that appears to contradict their official values.

This underside can provide outlets for what the official values exclude, helping people live with the wider social order. Žižek calls this the “obscene supplement”: the provocative and discomforting underbelly that a society struggles to acknowledge even while relying on it.
Victorian spiritualism helps us understand how this obscene supplement could become commercially productive.
The rise of modern spiritualism

Spiritualism is the belief that the dead can be contacted through people known as mediums. It emerged in the US in the late 1840s, following claims from self-styled mediums the Fox sisters that spirits communicated with them through mysterious knocks.

Spiritualism reached Britain through visiting American mediums. Seances, public demonstrations, specialist publications and objects such as “spirit cabinets” helped create a movement with its own celebrities and commercial networks.

An article appeared in The Times in 1872 expressing surprise that among “a generation which boasts itself to be one of exact science”, spiritualism had developed such interest. In our interpretation, spiritualism offered access to something apparently missing from a society increasingly focused on producing, acquiring and displaying “things”: evidence that there was more to life than the material world. Yet spiritualism seemed to make that offer through more things: paid encounters, purchasable photographs and advertised products.

This is where Žižek’s obscene supplement becomes revealing. A society’s apparent opposites can provide ways of living with its demands without fundamentally changing them. Spiritualism offered an escape from Victorian commercial culture while drawing people into new forms of consumption. Making that offer convincing required careful management.
Making the impossible marketable

Spiritualist publications warned that mediumship could not be bought. Nevertheless, mediums had livelihoods, publishers needed subscribers and organisers needed to cover costs. Mediumship was therefore presented as an exhausting and often dangerous duty whose selfless practitioners deserved to be paid fairly for their services.

To protect the movement’s brand, mediums such as Daniel Dunglas Home would publicly refuse direct payment for seances. Instead, he accepted gifts, hospitality, travel opportunities and material support from wealthy patrons, while other mediums requested expenses and a moderate fee proportionate to their clients’ means. Commerce became easier to accept when presented as support for a higher calling.

The same tension appeared in spiritualist publishing. Periodicals such as the Medium and Daybreak could devote their opening pages to condemning materialism and warning readers against excessive attachment to worldly possessions, only to fill their back pages with advertisements for dubious remedies, elixirs and quasi-scientific products marketed to those very readers. Spiritualism’s critique of consumer culture actually helped generate further opportunities for consumption.

Scientific credibility also required balancing. Spiritualists welcomed scientists’ involvement, approximated scientific and philosophical language, and used technical equipment to make extraordinary claims appear worthy of serious attention.

Photography was particularly useful. A supposedly objective technology could produce images presented as evidence of spirits. Its dependence on darkroom processes also supplied a useful analogy for why seances required darkness. An account in Medium and Daybreak described a photographic seance near Newcastle in 1880. The correspondent alludes to the importance of darkness, not to conceal any trickery but to mitigate the “trying effect of daylight” on ghosts’ “materialisation”.
The ghosts of Victorian capitalism still haunt us

The Victorian fascination with communicating beyond the grave may seem distant from our technologically sophisticated present. Yet contemporary forms of “digital necromancy” reveal a remarkably familiar tension: the desire to transcend the limits of human existence continues to generate new income streams.

As with Victorian mediums, today’s grief-tech entrepreneurs operate within a delicate relationship between emotional need, technological credibility and commercial legitimacy. The promise of connection may be sincerely offered and deeply meaningful to those who seek it, even as that same promise becomes a source of profit.
Perhaps this is the more unsettling legacy of Victorian spiritualism: desires that appear to challenge a society’s dominant values may, in fact, help sustain the very structures they seem to resist.
Rather than unsettling the established order, they can create new opportunities for its continued flourishing. The ghosts of Victorian capitalism, it seems, have never quite stopped doing business.

articles.title: How El Niño could push up your mortgage and grocery bills
articles.author: Narmin Nahidi, Assistant Professor in Finance, University of Exeter
paras: This year’s El Niño, the natural weather phenomenon that drives variations in temperature and winds across the Pacific, has prompted the UK government to pledge £15 million to help vulnerable countries such as Malawi, Kenya and Zambia prepare for droughts, floods and food shortages.
But the UK’s economic response will go beyond international aid. The Bank of England has identified El Niño as one of the key factors that could increase food inflation in 2027.

This connection between a climate pattern in the Pacific Ocean and supermarket prices (and possibly interest rates) in the UK is a clear demonstration of how extreme weather is an economic issue as well as an environmental one.

Environmentally speaking, the effects of El Niño can be devastating, bringing severe drought to some regions and severe flooding to others. And a stronger El Niño has a larger influence on global weather patterns than a weaker one.

This year’s event, already the strongest on record, is expected to peak later this year, and could cause global economic problems if it has a negative effect on major agricultural producers or transport routes.
Poor harvests can cause international agricultural prices to rise. Higher energy costs can simultaneously make fertiliser, processing and transportation more expensive.
The UK is particularly exposed to climate-related disruptions because of the international nature of its food supply (about 42% of its food is imported).

But these effects are rarely immediate. Many food manufacturers and retailers use risk management techniques to limit their exposure to sudden changes in prices, which can initially shield consumers from international shocks.
The Bank of England made this point explicitly, saying the potential effects of El Niño are likely to emerge gradually, rather than causing widespread food shortages or dramatic price rises.
And the central bank of Spain found that the effect of El Niño varies according to commodity, time period and agricultural policy.

For the most part, disasters with regard to food supply can be avoided with the right kind of human intervention. Businesses adapt. Farmers change production decisions. Trade shifts towards alternative suppliers. Governments intervene.
El Niño should therefore be viewed as a potential source of risk and volatility, rather than as a confident prediction that UK food prices must rise.
But what happens when several external shocks occur together?
The Bank of England has considered this possibility too, warning that a strong El Niño alongside renewed energy disruption could put much greater pressure on UK food prices.

If extreme weather also affects major shipping routes, the effects on import prices could become stronger still. This is where a climate event potentially becomes a monetary policy problem, as central banks treat El Niño as a factor that may cause them to raise interest rates.

In a recent meeting, the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee identified severe El Niño conditions as one possible source of additional pressure on agricultural prices, alongside energy markets and other global supply risks.

And this perhaps explains the thinking behind the UK government’s plan to help countries prepare for El Niño. The £15 million pledge announced in September 2026 is based on the idea of “anticipatory action”: releasing money before a predictable emergency rather than waiting until the economic damage has occurred.
The government says around 35% of humanitarian shocks can be predicted in advance, while less than 1% of global humanitarian funding currently goes towards anticipatory action.
There is a broader financial principle at work here.
If climate forecasts contain economically useful information, financial decisions can respond before losses actually occur.

So food importers can reconsider commodity and currency strategies to guard against shocks. Banks can incorporate weather-related supply disruption into their financial evaluations, and companies can stress-test supply chains against simultaneous commodity, energy and transportation shocks.
Governments can connect climate forecasting more closely with food security and planning for economic resilience.

And while they may not be able to predict exactly what El Niño will do to the price of a shopping basket, they can certainly act in a way that recognises the fact that information about future weather has financial value.

The UK government has shown that it is using weather forecasts to release humanitarian finance before disasters happen overseas. Those forecasts no longer provide key information just for meteorologists, farmers and fishing boats.
Increasingly, they contain vital financial data.

articles.title: The psychology that can lead investors to make bad financial decisions
articles.author: Donald Amuah, Lecturer in Accounting and Finance, University of South Wales
paras: Say you buy shares in a company. The price climbs and months later you sell for a healthy profit. Ask why it worked, and the answer is often some version of “I made a good call”. Now imagine the trade had lost money instead. Would you be as quick to blame your own judgment? Many of us wouldn’t. We may point to bad timing, a jittery market, anything but ourselves.
Psychologists call this “self-attribution bias”. Crediting ourselves for good outcomes, blaming something else for bad ones.

This bias matters more now that trading apps have made it easier for people with no formal training in finance to manage their own investments. Many of these apps offer tax-efficient accounts, such as stocks and shares Isas and self-invested personal pensions. They promote the tax advantages alongside low fees and sign-up incentives.
My colleagues and I explore this in our latest study, which examines self-attribution alongside two related biases – overconfidence and loss aversion – among people training to work in finance.

Behavioural finance exists as a subject because traditional theory, which assumes investors act rationally, struggles to explain why markets are prone to bubbles, or why we cling to losing positions long after we should sell. Self-attribution, overconfidence (an inflated sense of our ability relative to others) and loss aversion (feeling a loss more keenly than an equivalent gain) sit at the centre of it.

It’s a subject now taught at more than 40 UK universities. Yet there’s been surprisingly little research into teaching students to recognise these biases in their own decisions, rather than just learning the theory.
Knowledge doesn’t make us immune

We studied the financial decisions of 72 postgraduate students taking an MSc in finance and investment at the University of South Wales. They came from a range of countries, mainly Nigeria, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. Most were in their 30s or older. About 40% had never traded with real money.

Over four weeks, the students learned about trading psychology and then took part in a series of simulated trading exercises. This research project ended with a final trading game that counted towards their assessment. They also completed questionnaires and looked back at their own trading decisions to identify possible biases.

Before the final trading game, we asked students how well they expected to perform. Afterwards, we asked whether their actual result reflected their own trading skill. The difference was striking. More than 80% of students who performed better than expected said their result reflected their skill.
Among those who performed worse than expected, only about 16% said the same. Overall, nearly 70% of students acknowledged that they tended to take more credit for success than for failure.

We also found signs of overconfidence. For example, 84% of students expected to finish in the top half of the group, even though, by definition, no more than half could do so. Even among students who said they rarely followed financial news, everyone rated their understanding of it as at least “fair”.

We also found evidence of loss aversion. Students were asked to imagine two coin flips, risking £25 on one and £100 on the other, and named the smallest prize that would make each worth playing. Across both flips, around 75% asked for more than they stood to lose (indicating loss aversion), broadly in line with findings from research involving people in 53 countries.
It would be reassuring to think people studying for a finance masters – several with real trading experience already – would be less susceptible to these bases. Our results suggest otherwise.

That does not prove financial knowledge makes no difference. We did not compare this group with people who had no financial background. And we measured them once, not as their expertise grew as time progressed.

But it does show that technical, theoretical knowledge of markets was not, by itself, enough to stop these tendencies appearing. These biases are not really about what you know. They are about how the mind processes wins, losses and uncertainty, often automatically, before conscious reasoning gets a look in.

There was, however, an encouraging sign after a structured sequence of exercises, comparing predictions against outcomes, reviewing their own trading data and reflecting on decisions. The self-rated understanding of all three biases by students improved significantly.

It is important to note that this measured how well students felt they understood the biases, not their actual knowledge or behaviour. Feeling more aware of a bias is not the same as reliably avoiding it. As the study itself notes, insight is a start, but it doesn’t guarantee different decisions.

None of this means investors are doomed to be led astray by their own psychology, but simply knowing the theory isn’t enough. What seemed to help our students was structure. In other words, writing down what they expected before deciding, then honestly comparing it with what happened, reviewing their own trading history for patterns rather than trusting memory, and also setting rules for buying and selling in advance, not in the heat of the moment.

None of that requires a finance degree. For anyone managing their own pension or investments, the lesson may be simple – be wary of any story where your wins are always down to skill and your losses always down to bad luck.

articles.title: Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work
articles.author: Kenneth Greene, Professor of Government, The University of Texas at Austin
paras: Politics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win.

President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “DOGE dividend” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, rebates from tariff revenues, and a diversion of money currently used to subsidize health insurance companies directly to Americans.

But his pledge to give US$5,000 to every U.S. citizen if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which raises concerns from a legal point of view.

For this to actually happen, it needs congressional approval – and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where margins are tight in key races.

I’m a political scientist who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote.
Why vote buying rarely works

The practice dates back to ancient Rome and was a staple of American political machines from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia.

By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as newly arrived immigrants. Institutional reforms, including the professionalization of government bureaucracies at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s.
But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least 73 countries offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes.

If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the vote-buying attempts across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence.

Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are truly indifferent.

As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “Against the Machine.”
The importance of competition
There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops.

First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments influence voters’ responses to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party – and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts – you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights.

This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos.”

The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them moving targets: Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision.

Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret.

It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment.

Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it.
Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely.

Partisanship, a core element that makes people resistant to vote buying, is very strong in the U.S. electorate. There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while committed Democrats will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism.
The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.”

At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vote to Republican.

In theory, there is one way Trump’s offer could succeed. Research shows that buying turnout, rather than trying to change vote choices, is routinely effective. But all the examples come from countries where party officials actively monitor who comes to the polls. Without that surveillance, which is illegal in the U.S., the free-rider problem could bedevil turnout as well.

But whether enacted or not, the promise of cash for votes has a big downside for democracy. It means that no one will know whether victorious Republican candidates won this November because Americans preferred their policies and gave them a mandate – or because they expected to get paid.
Kenneth Greene's research has been funded by the National Science Foundation, the University of Texas at Austin, and the Mellon Foundation.

articles.title: More young people are being recruited as ‘money mules’ by organised crime groups, new analysis reveals
articles.author: Nicholas Ryder, Professor of Law, Cardiff University
paras: More than 8,900 people aged under 30 were arrested for money laundering offences in England and Wales between 2020 and 2025. That’s more than six in ten of all money laundering arrests recorded during the period.

And our analysis of police data points to a growing problem that is not simply about young people committing financial crime. It also reveals how organised crime groups are recruiting young people as “money mules”. These are people who move or receive criminal funds on behalf of others.
The UK government already recognises the threat posed by money mule networks. The 2025 national risk assessment identified schools and universities as an emerging risk.

Students appear to be particularly vulnerable. The police officers we interviewed for our report said young people can be targeted because they may be under financial pressure, lack experience in managing money or be unaware of the risks of becoming involved in money laundering. International students were considered especially vulnerable, with officers reporting that some are targeted soon after arriving in the UK.

A money mule may be asked to receive funds into their bank account and transfer it elsewhere, sometimes in return for payment. They may not realise where the money came from or understand that what they are doing is a criminal offence.

Our analysis of data obtained from 36 police forces through freedom of information requests found 14,493 money laundering arrests between January 2020 and January 2025. Of these, 8,956 involved people aged 18 to 29. A further 776 under-18s were recorded by 35 forces.

These figures do not tell us how many of those arrested were students. Police forces do not routinely record student status, so age is only an imperfect indication of involvement in education. But the scale of youth involvement is clear.

Students are vulnerable to acting as a money mules because they face financial pressures, are engaged with social media and lack awareness of the legal consequences of acting as a money mule. Organised crime groups have exploited these factors by using fake job advertisements and online recruitment tactics that promise easy income in exchange for using personal bank accounts to transfer funds.

International students may be especially vulnerable due to their need for UK bank accounts and cross-border financial activity. As a result, students can become unwitting participants in laundering the proceeds of fraud and organised crime. As one police officer told us “as soon as international students land in the UK … they are inundated with messages about money laundering”.

The data also reveals large differences between police forces. Money laundering arrests were concentrated in some of the UK’s largest urban areas. However, this may reflect differences in the scale of organised crime, financial activity and police resources. It may also reflect differences in how forces record offences.

More broadly, our report suggests that the criminal justice system is better equipped to deal with relatively straightforward money laundering cases than the more complex networks behind them. This is important because focusing on the person who moves the money can obscure the people directing the operation.

Young people recruited as money mules may be involved at the lowest level of a much larger criminal enterprise. Some may knowingly participate. Others may be manipulated, exploited or persuaded that what they are doing is harmless.
Our report noted that universities can be exposed to money laundering in a number of ways including through payments of fees or donations – thus unknowingly facilitating money laundering by students.

Yet universities are not currently covered by the UK’s money laundering regulations 2017 in the same way as regulated sectors such as banks, lawyers and accountants. That means universities do not have the same general obligations to identify and report suspected money laundering.

Our previous research illustrated that universities are susceptible to money laundering due to large financial flows and receipt of cash payments for tuition and accommodation fees. That research also found that over 20% of universities do not provide any anti-money laundering guidance to their students.

In our interviews and surveys with regional organised crime units and the City of London Police, we found uncertainty about how the rules apply to higher education. This can leave police focusing on the person receiving or transferring illicit money, rather than on potential risks within the institution or the wider criminal network.

Police interviewees described shortages of staff, specialist expertise and investigative resources. Some said economic crime could become a forgotten area when police forces are dealing with competing priorities.

Relationships between police forces and universities also varied considerably. In some areas, there were established local contacts and effective partnerships. In others, cooperation depended on individual relationships rather than a consistent national approach.
This fragmented response is particularly problematic when criminal networks operate across police force boundaries.

Our analysis does not suggest that universities are routinely being used to launder money. Nor can it establish how many students are involved in recorded money laundering offences. The available data has limitations, including differences in how police forces record offences.
But our findings point to a clear gap between the scale of the problem and the information available about it.
Our analysis points to four priorities.

First, universities should be brought within the money laundering regulations. This would give higher education institutions clear responsibilities for identifying and reporting suspected money laundering.

Second, prevention needs to start earlier and be more targeted. Universities should include money-mule awareness in student induction programmes, alongside financial education and social media campaigns. International students, who may be unfamiliar with the risks and the UK banking system, should receive particular support.

Third, universities and police forces need stronger partnerships. Sharing information and building established links could help identify suspicious activity and patterns of recruitment before individual cases become part of a larger criminal investigation.

Finally, the Home Office should develop a dedicated national strategy for money laundering and money-mule activity in educational settings. A consistent approach would help address the uneven enforcement, resources and relationships between police forces that our report identified.

Our report suggests that tackling money laundering effectively means looking beyond the person whose bank account receives the money. Young people may be the most visible part of the problem. But they are not necessarily the ones at the heart of it.

articles.title: The UK autumn budget: why the chancellor’s options are  limited
articles.author: Steve Schifferes, Honorary Research Fellow, City Political Economy Research Centre, City St George's, University of London
paras: The autumn budget looks set to be a cautious affair. It is not expected to spark the kind of Labour party enthusiasm that Andy Burnham has enjoyed in his first three months as prime minister.

In that short time, Burnham has promised not to shy away from tackling the big issues facing the UK, such as social care, weak economic growth and the effects of Brexit. He says he also wants to offer immediate and tangible help to those who are struggling with the cost of living.

But it is not clear how much help his chancellor John Healey can afford to offer. And much of what he can afford will end up being paid for by cuts to spending elsewhere, because the overall economic picture in the UK is so mixed.
The country’s growth forecast, for example, was recently raised by the IMF slightly to 1.3% for next year. This is better than for most G7 countries, but still weak by historic standards.
And the IMF is also predicting higher inflation in the UK, which could lead the Bank of England to raise interest rates, slowing growth.

With the UK being an export-led economy, weak growth in the EU (its largest trading partner by far) could dampen economic prospects, despite Burnham’s overtures to reset relations. Elsewhere, there is always a chance that the ongoing war between the US and Iran could cause more damage to the world economy.

The chancellor’s options are limited by competing pressures. How does he provide more help to voters, especially on energy bills, while avoiding increasing taxes that would damage business confidence and reduce growth prospects?
He has already ruled out any changes to capital gains taxes, which are currently taxed at a lower rate than income tax, on the grounds that it would inhibit investment and reduce economic growth.

As ever, looming over Healey’s decisions is the fear that the bond market would react negatively to any further increases in borrowing, with total government debt of £3 trillion, almost the size of the entire British economy. Interest rates on government bonds are already at record highs.
The bill for interest repayment for this financial year alone is already forecast to be twice the size of the defence budget.

That said, the IMF has praised the UK for having a credible plan to reduce its debt. The government’s fiscal rules are designed to bring spending and tax revenues into balance over three years. The chancellor will be extremely reluctant to sacrifice his credibility by any major changes to the fiscal rules that could lead to increases in the government’s debt.
His “fiscal headroom” (the extra money the chancellor might be able to spend while still meeting his fiscal rules) has already been reduced by rising spending and weaker tax receipts.

This leaves the government with a choice of either cutting spending or raising taxes to fund more help with the cost of living. For example, any subsidy for energy bills is likely to be limited to those on benefits and could be funded by cuts to the existing energy budget.

Businesses have protested vigorously against any further tax increases, following the increase in companies’ national insurance payments introduced by former chancellor Rachel Reeves. And while Healey seems to be considering increased taxes on the highly profitable banking sector, he may frame this as a down payment on increases to defence spending.

The biggest long-term challenges facing the chancellor are how to fund social care, how to manage the redistribution of tax revenues to the devolved regions, and how to fund a major increase in the defence budget – the very issue that Healey resigned from his previous role as defence secretary over.

But it appears that all of these will be kicked into the long grass until next year’s government spending review. This will set out the government’s spending plans for the next three years running up to the next general election.
In the meantime, a steady-as-you-go budget will please the bond markets and industry. But it could fall short of reassuring the public that the government is really on their side.

articles.title: Wild fish are a precious resource – here’s how aquaculture can bolster food security
articles.author: Wesley Malcorps, Research Fellow, Institute of Aquaculture, University of Stirling
paras: Small fish such as sardinella are an affordable source of protein and essential nutrients for millions of people across West Africa.

Some of these fish are increasingly exported or processed into fishmeal and fish oil for aquaculture feeds used in high-income European countries and across East Asia, particularly China. As nutrient deficiencies are common in people living in parts of West Africa, retaining more fish for local consumption could help improve diets and address dietary health problems.

Aquaculture is one of the world’s fastest-growing food production sectors. Despite its growth in the last three decades, global wild fish catches for marine ingredients have declined overall. Production has increased in some regions, including West Africa, but the overall decline is mainly due to improved fishery management that allows recovery of fish stocks.

Globally, a quarter of wild-caught fish are processed into fishmeal and fish oil, and only a small share originates from West Africa. Most is used in animal feed, with aquaculture accounting for the largest share. These provide valuable nutrients, particularly in early-life-stage diets and for carnivorous species such as salmon and shrimp, while contributing to the relatively low carbon footprint of farmed seafood.

The supply of marine ingredients is highly regulated and fairly stable but should not be taken for granted. Climate change and warming periods such as El Niño can weaken the upwelling of nutrient-rich waters from the deep sea. This reduces the availability of plankton and fish and limits the supply of marine ingredients required for aquaculture.

This means we need to make the best use of the resources already available. Fish processing by-products (including heads, guts and skeletons) are playing an increasingly important role, accounting for 34% of global fishmeal production and 54% of fish oil supply in 2024.
A new era of supply chain risk

Marine ingredients from potentially unsustainable sources have slipped through the net despite responsible sourcing claims. One 2025 investigation found that certified Turkish-farmed seabass sold by major retailers in Europe was fed fishmeal sourced from three factories in Senegal that have been linked to food insecurity and job losses in local communities.

One way to reduce risk in aquaculture feed supply chains is to source ingredients domestically. But this is easier said than done. Aquafeed supply chains are dependent on the global trade in marine and terrestrial ingredients and thus face challenges related to scale, cost, nutritional quality and environmental sustainability.

While marine ingredients can be sustainably sourced and continue to be essential to the global food system, it’s important to use them in efficient ways that maximise their contribution to human nutrition. Certification programmes currently focus on ensuring that fish are caught or farmed responsibly. The environmental and social safeguards include stock status, environmental footprint and making sure workers are treated fairly.

The certification programmes pay less attention to food security and critics argue they favour export markets and corporations over local communities. As a result, calls are growing for broader measures of what constitutes truly sustainable and ethical seafood.

Some scientists argue that fish, such as anchovies and mackerel, provide more essential nutrients when eaten directly rather than used as feed. Most species used in the marine ingredients industry have low market appeal and limited consumer demand, meaning that diverting fish from feed to food does not automatically improve food security.

Peru’s anchoveta fishery is the world’s largest fish stock used to produce marine ingredients. Despite its scale and nutritional value, there has been low demand for anchoveta as a food fish within Peru. Factors such as low demand, short shelf life, limited logistics and strong economic incentives to process fish into fishmeal and fish oil have often hindered the development of markets for some fish as food. Strategic use of some fish as feed can help convert marine resources into nutritious and accessible seafood.

To make the most of limited marine resources, the aquaculture industry could improve how it tracks fish and nutrients as they are transformed into farmed seafood. We have developed a novel peer-reviewed performance tool that provides a common sustainability language. At the heart of the tool is the Fish In: Fish Out (Fifo) ratio, a measure of how efficiently fish, and the omega-3 fatty acids they contain, are converted into farmed fish.

Efficiency can be improved by increasing the use of fish processing by-products that are not normally eaten by people and by strategically replacing certain marine ingredients with alternatives such as algal oil and insect meal. The tool is currently being used by a variety of organisations like feed and ingredient companies, farmers, environmental charities, and researchers.

Applying the tool in our latest study already challenged conventional thinking about marine ingredient use in aquaculture. Although Faroese salmon is often viewed as a major consumer of marine ingredients, we found it was actually a net producer of edible omega-3 fatty acids. This was achieved by upcycling valuable nutrients from inedible sources (fishery by-products) into a nutritious farmed product, without increasing the need for fish that could be consumed directly by humans.

Making the most of limited marine resources is important, but decisions made in one country can affect food availability and affordability elsewhere. Therefore, harmonising nutrition-sensitive policies across local, national and regional levels is crucial to achieve meaningful outcomes. Traceability systems can play an important role, but they must do more than track supply chains.

They can only make a meaningful difference when they empower local communities through greater participation in decision-making and improved market access. They should support those closest to the resource, rather than treating them simply as sources of data for downstream companies. In West Africa, this could include retaining a proportion of the catch for local consumption and improving the cold chain to support its distribution.

These approaches would enable the marine ingredients and aquaculture industries to operate effectively. They would also contribute more to global food security, the economy and the supply of nutritious seafood to consumers.

Wesley Malcorps is Co-Founder and CEO of Blue Food Performance and provides consulting services to the seafood sector, including the development of sustainability assessments, strategies, dashboards and tools. As part of his academic work, he also receives funding from a variety of sources that support research and innovation activities.

Richard Newton is a founder of BFP and advisor on sustainability assessments. He has previously received funding from the EU, CIEL and IFFO to work on aspects of improving circular aspects of marine ingredients production.

articles.title: Jackdaw approval: what a new North Sea gasfield means for UK energy security, bills and tax
articles.author: Karl Matikonis, Assistant Professor in Taxation, University College Dublin
paras: The UK government has just approved the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, clearing the way for production to begin as early as this winter.
Jackdaw, around 150 miles east of Aberdeen, could account for roughly 6.5% of UK North Sea gas production at its peak and will connect to existing infrastructure at the Shearwater platform.
But what will this actually mean for households and public finances? Will Jackdaw lower energy bills? Probably not by any noticeable amount.

Producing more British gas may sound as though it should lower prices. But North Sea gas is not reserved for British consumers at a special domestic price. It is sold into a market connected to Europe and influenced by international gas prices. This was clear following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Britain continued producing gas domestically, yet consumers were still exposed to soaring international wholesale prices.

According to one analysis, even if Britain maximised North Sea production and returned all resulting government revenues to households, the average annual saving would be no more than £82. Jackdaw is one field, so its effect would be small.
Will this new gas field licence improve energy security? Here the case is stronger.

Britain consumes more gas than it produces and increasingly depends on imports as older North Sea fields decline. Jackdaw will not make Britain energy independent, but additional domestic production can reduce imports.

There is an important distinction between security of supply and protection from high prices. Jackdaw can contribute to the first, but not the second while consumers remain exposed to international gas prices.

In terms of how much tax Jackdaw will generate, North Sea taxes are currently charged on profits, not total sales. Investment reliefs (tax breaks that allow companies to deduct certain investment costs) can reduce those taxable profits.

Companies can generally deduct day-to-day operating costs when calculating taxable profits. They can also claim tax relief for certain development costs, investments to reduce emissions and, eventually, the costs of dismantling the field.

For Jackdaw, development investment will be in the region of £2.1 billion according to Adura, the UK North Sea’s largest independent oil and gas producer. Yet using the developer’s production forecast which estimates of how much gas and other products Jackdaw will produce each year, and the UK government’s Office for Budget Responsibility’s March 2026 oil and gas price assumptions, we estimate Jackdaw would generate only around £1.5 billion to £1.6 billion in gross sales by the end of 2029. Around £1 billion would come from gas, with the remainder from condensate and natural gas liquids (these are the liquid products extracted alongside natural gas that are sold separately).
Based on this simple comparison, gross sales through 2029 would still be below the project’s implied development investment, even before operating costs are taken into account.

This does not mean Jackdaw will pay no tax. Public information does not reveal how much investment qualifies for tax relief, when allowances will be used or how Jackdaw fits into the operator’s wider North Sea tax position. Adura estimates that Jackdaw and the much larger Rosebank project together could generate around £1.4 billion in tax by mid-2029 but does not say how much of that would come from Jackdaw.

There is another complication. The energy profits levy (a temporary 38% tax on oil and gas profits) is due to end by March 2030. It will be replaced by the oil and gas revenue levy, a new tax that would apply when oil and gas prices rise above specified levels. Unlike the current windfall tax, this would charge 35% on revenues above specified price thresholds, regardless of a field’s costs. My research suggests the same revenue threshold can affect high- and low-cost fields very differently.
What Jackdaw really changes

Jackdaw will not give Britain cheap gas or make the country energy independent. Its significance is more limited: it can replace some imported gas and support economic activity, but Britain will remain exposed to international gas prices.

The financial picture is similarly complicated. A 78% headline tax rate does not mean 78% of Jackdaw’s revenues will reach the Treasury. Investment reliefs can reduce tax in a field’s early years, while jobs and supply-chain activity generate other tax revenues and eventual decommissioning costs can also qualify for tax relief.

These benefits must be weighed against the emissions and environmental costs of further fossil-fuel production, and against investing instead in renewables, storage and other ways of reducing dependence on gas.
By producing a little more of its own gas, Britain can marginally improve its security of energy supply, but this won’t lower prices or guarantee an immediate tax windfall.

articles.title: US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect
articles.author: Markus Schneider, Associate Professor of Economics, University of Denver
paras: The buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections may be affordability, but growing anger over inequality is behind the sentiment.

A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans – including 4 in 10 Republicans – believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this.

This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs.

I’m an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices – including taxation and public spending – enabled this 40-year rise in inequality.

Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%.

Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow. The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999.

These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data.

But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026.
Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories.

Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall. The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom.
Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive, often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats.

The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – including international studies – doesn’t back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth.

Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940.

It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from.

Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership, allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash, usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares.

By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%.
The new drivers of inequality

Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed.

One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs.

The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil.

Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%.

This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “A Brief History of Equality,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.”
